Question 1)

A) first lets get the distribution needed using r norm. 100 observations with a mean of 0 and a sd of 2.
 sample variance = 4.174892. sample sd = 2.043255. 

```{r}
en_oh_two <- rnorm(100, 0, 2)
var(en_oh_two)
sd(en_oh_two)
```

# now to create and run population variance function. Using population formula we get variance = 4.133143
```{r}
pop_var <- function(x) {
  n = length(x)
  sum((x - mean(x))^2) / length(x)
}
  
pop_var(en_oh_two)
```

now lets run it using a simulated sample of 10 observations. This gives us variance = 3.870828
```{r}
check <- rnorm(10, 0, 2)

pop_var(check)
```


1.B) get the distribution then apply the function. Population variance of sample is in df q1b.vp. 
```{r}
q1b <- replicate(1000, rnorm(5, 0, 2))

# wait but now this is inverted. transpose?

q1b <- t(q1b)

# ok. now create new df with pop-var for each row
q1b.vp  <- data.frame(pop.var  = apply(q1b, 1, pop_var))
```


Now plotting the sampling distribution of both measures. Plot is below. True variance is marked by solid black line while dashed blue line shows variance derived from population formula. It is to the left of the true variance
```{r}
ggplot(data = q1b.vp, mapping = aes(x = pop.var)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = 'lavender') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4, colour = 'black', linetype = 'solid') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(q1b.vp$pop.var), colour = 'blue', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_density(colour = "black", size = 1) +
  labs("Note: Solid black line = true variance. Dashed blue line = population variance.") +
  theme_classic()

```

Meanwhile, graph of distribution of variance values derived from sample formula is below. Dashed line is VERY close to the true variance. We can safely conclude that the most biased estimator is the population variance formula. It has negative bias.
```{r}
q1b.vp2 <- data.frame(samp.var = apply(q1b, 1, var))

# plot
ggplot(data = q1b.vp2, mapping = aes(x = samp.var)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = 'lavender') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4, colour = 'black', linetype = 'solid') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(q1b.vp2$samp.var), colour = 'blue', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_density(colour = "black", size = 1) +
  labs("Note: Solid black line = true variance. Dashed blue line = sample variance.") +
  theme_classic()
```

1.C) 3, 5, 10, 30, 100. Scatterplot below. Estimated bias decreases as sample size increases
```{r}
three <- replicate(3, rnorm(5, 0, 2))
five <- replicate(5, rnorm(5, 0, 2))
ten <- replicate(10, rnorm(5, 0, 2))
thirty <- replicate(30, rnorm(5, 0, 2))
hundred <- replicate(1000, rnorm(5, 0, 2))

three.vp  <- data.frame(pop.var  = apply(three, 1, pop_var))
vp.3.av <- data.frame(mean(three.vp$pop.var))
vp.3.av$size <- 3
vp.3.av$bias <- vp.3.av$mean.three.vp.pop.var. - 4

five.vp  <- data.frame(pop.var  = apply(five, 1, pop_var))
vp.5.av <- data.frame(mean(five.vp$pop.var))
vp.5.av$size <- 5
vp.5.av$bias <- vp.5.av$mean.five.vp.pop.var. - 4

ten.vp  <- data.frame(pop.var  = apply(ten, 1, pop_var))
vp.10.av <- data.frame(mean(ten.vp$pop.var))
vp.10.av$size <- 10
vp.10.av$bias <- vp.10.av$mean.ten.vp.pop.var. - 4

thirty.vp  <- data.frame(pop.var  = apply(thirty, 1, pop_var))
vp.30.av <- data.frame(mean(thirty.vp$pop.var))
vp.30.av$size <- 30
vp.30.av$bias <- vp.30.av$mean.thirty.vp.pop.var. - 4

hundred.vp  <- data.frame(pop.var  = apply(hundred, 1, pop_var))
vp.100.av <- data.frame(mean(hundred.vp$pop.var))
vp.100.av$size <- 100
vp.100.av$bias <- vp.100.av$mean.hundred.vp.pop.var. - 4

# need to standardize the names of popvar columns
names(vp.3.av)[1]   <- "mean.popvar"
names(vp.5.av)[1]   <- "mean.popvar"
names(vp.10.av)[1]  <- "mean.popvar"
names(vp.30.av)[1]  <- "mean.popvar"
names(vp.100.av)[1] <- "mean.popvar"

pop_var_graph_data <- rbind(vp.3.av, vp.5.av, vp.10.av, vp.30.av, vp.100.av)

# finally we plot now
ggplot(data = pop_var_graph_data, mapping = aes(x = size, y = bias)) +
  geom_point(colour = 'purple') +
  labs(x = "Sample Size", y = "Estimated Bias") +
  theme_classic()
```

1.E) When comparing the standard deviation of the variance estimators, it becomes clear that the population formula presents less variation. Still, this does not make it a superior estimator, because it contains much higher bias. While this estimator is more consistent, the sample formula clusters around the same mean as our parameter as both measures' sample size increases.
```{r}
sd(q1b.vp$pop.var)
sd(q1b.vp2$samp.var)

```


2.A) Dataset generated below. Distributions checked with hist() command. Correlation between xi and z in dataset is 0.492086. 
```{r}
# true model
rho <- 0.5
z <- rnorm(100, 0, 1)
ui <- rnorm(100, 0, 1)
ei <- rnorm(100, 0, 1)

b0 <- 1
b1 <- 2
b2 <- 3

b1_true <- 2

xi <- rho * z + sqrt(1-rho^2) * ui
yi <- b0 + b1*xi + b2*z + ei

# check distributions
hist(z)
hist(ui)
hist(ei)
hist(xi)
hist(yi)
cor(xi, z)

```


2.B)  Comparing findings from both models, it becomes clear that news consumption is positively associated with political knowledge at a statistically significant level. However, once we account for Political Interest (z), the coefficient for news consumption becomes smaller. Political Interest's effect size is also larger than news consumption's. In addition, ccounting for Interest greatly improveed the model's fit, since it's R-squared increased from 0.53 to 0.93. The second model's coefficeints are also much closer to the estimand. 
```{r}
# lets fit both models!
# first theorized mdoel
theorized_model <- lm(yi ~ xi)
summary(theorized_model)

true_model <- lm(yi ~ xi + z)
summary(true_model)

models_plot_df <- data_frame(xi, yi, z)

xy_plot <- ggplot(data = models_plot_df, mapping = aes(x = xi, y = yi)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() + 
  xlab('News Consumption') + 
  ylab('Political Knowledge')

xy_plot
```

2.C) More data brought the true model's B1 coefficient closer to the estimand. While more data also brought the theorized model's B1 coefficient slightly closer to the estimand, it was still far from it. In other words, it remained biased. 
```{r}
z_2 <- rnorm(1000, 0, 1)
ui_2 <- rnorm(1000, 0, 1)
ei_2 <- rnorm(1000, 0, 1)


xi_2 <- rho * z_2 + sqrt(1-rho^2) * ui_2
yi_2 <- b0 + b1*xi_2 + b2*z_2 + ei_2

# check distributions
hist(z_2)
hist(ui_2)
hist(ei_2)
hist(xi_2)
hist(yi_2)
cor(xi_2, z_2)

# models
theorized_model_2 <- lm(yi_2 ~ xi_2)
summary(theorized_model_2)

true_model_2 <- lm(yi_2 ~ xi_2 + z_2)
summary(true_model_2)
```

2.D) After repeating with rho = 0, the coefficient for B1 in the simple/theorized model is much closer to its actual value. In addition, the inclusion of z in the model did not alter the B1 coefficient or its level of statistical significance. Still, the R-squared is lower in the naive model. This means that, when constructing regression models, we should be very careful about our choice of control variables. As demonstrated here, including a control variable that has no correlation with x, and thus one which cannot serve as a confounding variable, but is still related to y could improve model fit but will have no impact on our variable of interest. This decision should depend on the researcher's objectives. Someone who is looking for higher precision would want to include the uncorrelated controls, while those who are primarily concerned about x's impact on y may not be well-served by including the set of controls. 
```{r}
rho_2 <- 0

xi_3 <- rho_2 * z_2 + sqrt(1-rho_2^2) * ui_2
yi_3 <- b0 + b1*xi_3 + b2*z_2 + ei_2

theorized_model_3 <- lm(yi_3 ~ xi_3)
summary(theorized_model_3)

true_model_3 <- lm(yi_3 ~ xi_3 + z_2)
summary(true_model_3)
```
